passages.label: A
passages.text: One tea plant can end up as several different drinks. Japan's agriculture ministry describes sencha as the most common type of Japanese green tea. It is made with leaves that workers pick, heat and dry before people prepare the drink at home, and the order of the work matters.

passages.label: B
passages.text: First, workers pick the leaves and put them in steam, and this keeps them from changing the way leaves for black tea do. Then the leaves cool. A machine rolls them, and they dry a little, and the workers do this more than once, and the last roll makes the leaves long and thin. The final drying takes out most of the water, and the rolling and drying do different jobs. Rolling helps change the shape of the leaves while drying takes away water, and the two jobs work together.

passages.label: C
passages.text: The taste of sencha can differ between two cups. Where the plants grow and when the leaves are picked can change it, and the time in the steam also makes a difference. A longer time can give a deeper green colour and a less sharp taste. The main steps stay the same.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Other teas use some of the same steps. Tencha is dried without rolling and can be ground into matcha. Heating sencha or bancha makes a drink with a warm smell. Brown rice can be mixed with some green teas, and the work after picking changes the final taste. The way tea is made and shared has become part of food culture.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Tea can go with a meal. People can enjoy it alongside fresh fish, noodles, a vegetable salad or a dish with a light sauce. A simple sandwich with bread works too. The same tea can be used with milk or honey, but the extra taste changes the drink. How a plant is grown matters as much as what is served with tea.

passages.label: A
passages.text: The Japanese agriculture ministry gives a clear method for making sencha in a kyusu, a Japanese teapot. Good tea is made with water at a temperature that suits the type of leaves. Before the water touches the leaves, the host can use the cups to measure the amount needed for all the guests. The ministry suggests boiling fresh water for three to five minutes and allowing it to cool.

passages.label: B
passages.text: For high-quality sencha, the guide suggests about 70 degrees Celsius. Average sencha can take hotter water, approximately 80 degrees, and a person can pour the hot water into each cup first. This warms the cups and cools the water at the same time, and the measured water also helps the host prepare the right amount for the group.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Next, the host puts tea leaves in the pot and pours in the cooled water. The leaves rest for one or two minutes, and the host should not shake the pot. When the tea is ready, the host pours a little into each cup, then repeats the order until the pot is empty, and this helps every guest receive a similar taste and strength.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Cooler water brings out a sweeter taste, and hot water may add bitterness. The host can enjoy trying different cups with the same leaves from a plant. A fresh sandwich or bread with jam can change what a guest notices. A guest who has just eaten fish, noodles or a vegetable salad may notice the tea differently. This is one reason to taste the drink by itself first.

passages.label: E
passages.text: The ministry's method suggests about three grams of leaves for each person. When the tea is served with a rice dish at a meal, the taste can matter as much as the food itself. Milk or honey would change the taste in a different way, so a useful comparison begins with an ordinary cup of the plain drink. After pouring, the host serves the last drop because it contains strong flavour.

passages.label: A
passages.text: What a visitor sees on an Australian menu can change from place to place. Some dishes are made with ingredients from native plants or animals, while other dishes reflect food brought from around the world. One type of food can be prepared in several different ways, and the names on a menu can tell part of that story.

passages.label: B
passages.text: Food from the sea includes barramundi, prawns, mussels and oysters. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people have gathered seafood for thousands of years. Today, a cook may prepare a fish dish with vegetables or a sauce and include it in a meal. A vegetable dish can be served with that meal.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Kangaroo is another native food. Tourism Australia says kangaroo meat is lean, high in protein, and taken from nature rather than farms. It has a strong flavour and appears on some seasonal menus. Crocodile meat is low in fat and high in protein, and these foods are examples, not foods that every Australian eats each day.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Plants add taste as well. Wattleseed can be ground into flour for damper, a type of bread. Lemon myrtle has a taste like lemon and saltbush tastes salty. A cook may use a leaf as a spice or as part of a drink. A small amount can be enough to change the flavour.

passages.label: E
passages.text: When people enjoy a meal, they can ask about its place in local culture. A cook may use a local plant in a salad, a vegetable dish or a peppery sauce for fresh fish. A sweet dish might use honey. A visitor can compare this with an international menu that includes noodles or a familiar sandwich. Names on a menu can be a starting point for asking where an ingredient comes from. A person who asks about a dish may hear who grew the leaves and when people first used them.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Why would eating at one restaurant give a visitor only part of the picture of Australian food?
options: A whole region can be understood from one meal if the visitor chooses locally grown food.
Most locations serve the same meals and vary only what they call them.
One restaurant can represent all places if its menu includes both meat and seafood.
What is put into a dish and how it is made can differ across locations.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: How does the passage connect the seafood gathered for thousands of years with what a visitor might eat now?
options: Food from the sea has a long local history and can be prepared as part of a meal today.
Only cooks following an unchanged recipe from the past serve this food today.
This food was collected long ago, but it is no longer an option for a meal.
A modern fish dish is presented as a replacement for earlier ways of obtaining seafood.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which answer shows one ingredient doing two different jobs without becoming the main dish?
options: Two meats can be compared by how much protein they contain.
A leaf can change the flavour of food or be used in a beverage.
Two types of seafood can be put next to each other on a list.
A vegetable dish can go beside a fish dish in the same meal.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What can a seasonal menu tell a visitor about kangaroo without showing what most people eat each day?
options: It tells the visitor that most people eat kangaroo on any day at home.
It shows that kangaroo is available at every restaurant in the country.
It shows kangaroo can be offered at certain times, without establishing how often people eat it.
It shows exactly how the meat is prepared in each season.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which comparison between kangaroo and crocodile is supported by the passage?
options: Both are described as high in protein. Only kangaroo is said here to come from the wild.
Both are described as having a strong flavour and coming from farms.
Crocodile is said to have more protein than kangaroo.
Both are described as low in fat, but only kangaroo is described as high in protein.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which detail about kangaroo meat could a diner notice by tasting it?
options: A salty taste like the leaf of a native plant.

A mild taste like a plain piece of bread.
A taste that is easy to notice.

options: A cook needs a large portion of the ingredient before a person can taste it.
A little of the ingredient can be enough to make the food taste different.
Adding a small amount is described as changing only how the dish looks.
Only the plants used to make flour can affect the taste of a dish.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What extra information can a question about a dish lead to?
options: The price a restaurant pays for every imported ingredient.
The exact time a fish dish was cooked at a restaurant.
Whether everyone in the country eats the dish regularly.
Who grew an ingredient and when people first used it.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: A diner wants to learn about the place through a meal. Which response best reflects the writer’s purpose?
options: Choose something unfamiliar and use it to ask what connects the ingredients to the people who live there.
Pick a dish that is familiar and treat it as a guide to what people usually eat throughout the country.
Choose the most unusual food and assume that every visitor is offered it in the same way.
Read the meat list to find which meal is served most often in every part of the country.
